warmup.q: A processor asks resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("Inventory"), with the annotation's short name, on a file with two classes marked @Inventory. What happens?
options: It finds nothing, and KSP prints no warning
KSP stops with an error about an unknown annotation
It finds every annotation whose name ends in Inventory
warmup.why: getSymbolsWithAnnotation compares fully qualified names, and no annotation is called just Inventory, so the honest answer is an empty list. Nothing warns. The first sign of trouble is later code that calls a card nobody generated. RungsDemo in the second section shows it: asked for "Inventory", found 0.

opening:
Picture the helper from the last lesson on their first morning. They have a clipboard, a pen, a house full of sealed boxes, and one instruction: every box with an @Inventory sticky note gets an inventory card. Before the first card, though, the moving company has to know the helper exists, and the helper has to know exactly which note to look for.

In the last lesson, we watched a ready-made processor write MoveMate's cards during the build, and we saw its two limits: it can't look inside a box, and it can't change one. Now we'll write that processor ourselves, rung by rung: one that only reports in, one that finds the notes, and one that writes a card for each class. Along the way we'll break it on purpose, five different ways, and read exactly what KSP prints each time. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a helper on their first morning, with a clipboard and one instruction. KSP found the helper through the services file, the helper found the notes by their full name, wrote one card per class, reported the interface on its exact line, and stopped writing when a round brought nothing new.

In a project of your own that uses KSP, open build/generated/ksp/main/kotlin after a build, and find one file that a processor wrote for you. Then find the class it came from.

Next, we'll read the rest of the label. What does KSP know about a type like Map<String, List<Int?>>?, and how do you print it without losing a question mark?

sections.h: The smallest processor KSP will run: a provider, a processor and a services file
sections.html:
An annotation is a note in the code written with @, such as @Inventory, MoveMate's sticky note for "make an inventory card for this one". An annotation processor is a program that runs during the build (the steps Gradle takes to turn your source files into a program), reads the annotated classes, and writes new source files. KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, runs such processors on Kotlin code.

A KSP processor is two small classes and one text file. The processor is the helper: a class that implements SymbolProcessor, whose process function KSP calls during the build. The provider is the moving company that sends the helper: a class that implements SymbolProcessorProvider, whose one job is to create the processor and hand it its tools. The services file is how KSP finds the company: a text file inside the processor's jar (the zip file a Java library ships in) that names the provider class.

Here's the first rung, a processor that only reports each pass it makes, with the closest Java equivalent first:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor (javax.annotation.processing)
@SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory")
@SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_21)
public class RoundLogger extends AbstractProcessor {     // javac creates it with new RoundLogger()
    private int round = 0;

    @Override
    public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) {
        round++;
        processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.WARNING, "round " + round);
        return false;                                     // don't claim @Inventory for this processor alone
    }
}
Kotlin
class RoundLoggerProvider : SymbolProcessorProvider {   // KSP finds this through the services file
    override fun create(environment: SymbolProcessorEnvironment): SymbolProcessor =
        RoundLogger(environment.logger)
}

class RoundLogger(private val logger: KSPLogger) : SymbolProcessor {
    override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true }
    private var round = 0

    override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> {
        round++
        logger.warn("round $round")
        return emptyList()                                // nothing set aside for a later round
    }
}

Let's walk through the Kotlin version from the top. KSP calls the provider's create once per build and passes it an environment, a bag of tools. codeGenerator writes files, logger prints messages, and options holds settings from the build file (lesson 7). Our processor keeps only the logger.

KSP then calls process with a Resolver, the helper's clipboard: it answers questions such as "which symbols carry this note?" process returns the symbols it couldn't handle yet, and an empty list means "all done". The apiFeatures line opts in to newer KSP behavior; without it, KSP 2.3.14 prints three notes on every run asking you to.

Java has had annotation processors like this one since Java 6, and KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do the same job for Kotlin code. Two things differ in the Java twin. Java has no provider: javac creates the processor itself, through a public constructor with no parameters. And @SupportedAnnotationTypes tells javac which annotations the processor wants, while every KSP processor simply sees every file.

The services file is one line, the provider's full class name:

workbench.ksp.l02.InventoryProcessorProvider

In an ordinary project it lives at src/main/resources/META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider. In this lab each lesson keeps its own copy, at src/main/resources/workbench/ksp/l02/SymbolProcessorProvider, and the build moves it to that path inside lesson 2's jar. Java's file has a different name, META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor, and the same job.

What happens without it? Empty the lab's file, keep it, and run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin -Pmine=l02:

> Task :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin FAILED
e: [ksp] No providers found in processor classpath.

Misspell the class name instead, and the build names the typo: Provider workbench.ksp.l02.InventoryProcessorProvidr not found. KSP is strict about this file, and that's a kindness: it fails at once, not three steps later.

Why does the processor live in its own module, a project of its own within the build (labs/ksp), and not next to MoveMate's classes in labs/ksp/app? Because it's a program that must be compiled before it can run on your code. If the app's KSP task needed the app's own compiled classes, each would wait for the other, and Gradle refuses such a loop with Circular dependency between the following tasks. So the processor sits in a module of its own, and the app adds it through the ksp configuration, a named list of dependencies that only KSP uses:

// app/build.gradle.kts in an ordinary project: the processor lives in a module of its own
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.21"
    id("com.google.devtools.ksp") version "2.3.14"
}

dependencies {
    implementation(project(":annotations"))    // the sticky notes: your code uses them
    ksp(project(":processor"))                 // the helper: only the build uses it
}

A processor is a provider, a processor and a services file. If KSP can't find all three, nothing runs.

Every processor in this track makes the same five moves, named the same way each time. Find the symbols with the note. Check that each one is something you can handle. Read the parts of its label you need. Write the new file. Prove it works, in tests and then in a real build. Rung one makes none of them yet; it only shows that KSP found the helper. Next, the helper should notice the sticky notes.

sections.h: Finding the sticky notes: getSymbolsWithAnnotation and the annotation's full name
sections.html:
Rung two asks the clipboard its first question. A symbol is anything in your code with a name: a class, a function, a property, a parameter. A declaration is a symbol you declared yourself, and a class declaration arrives as a KSClassDeclaration. KSP calls everything that can carry an annotation a KSAnnotated, and getSymbolsWithAnnotation returns those that carry the one you name:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: javac's RoundEnvironment
@Override
public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) {
    Messager messager = processingEnv.getMessager();
    TypeElement inventory = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getTypeElement("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory");
    Set<? extends Element> found = roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(inventory);
    messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.WARNING, "found " + found.size());
    for (Element element : found) {
        messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.WARNING, "found " + element.getSimpleName(), element);
    }
    return false;
}
Kotlin
override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> {
    val found = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory").toList()
    logger.warn("found ${found.size}")
    for (symbol in found) {
        if (symbol is KSClassDeclaration) logger.warn("found ${symbol.simpleName.asString()}", symbol)
    }
    return emptyList()
}

Both versions ask by the annotation's identity. Java looks up the annotation's TypeElement and passes it in. KSP takes the annotation's fully qualified name, its package and class name together, as a plain string. The second argument to logger.warn is the symbol itself, and that's worth making a habit: KSP then prints where the symbol is, its file and line.

RungsDemo runs rung one, this rung, and a variant that asks for the short name "Inventory", all on one MoveMate file. The file has two @Inventory classes and a Wardrobe without the note. Predict the three counts, then compare:

exit code: OK
w: [ksp] [rung 1] round 1
w: [ksp] [rung 2] asked for "workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory", found 2
w: [ksp] .../MoveMate.kt:6: [rung 2] found Lamp
w: [ksp] .../MoveMate.kt:9: [rung 2] found Plant
w: [ksp] [rung 2] asked for "Inventory", found 0

The full name found both classes, each with its file and line, and the wardrobe stayed out of it, as it should. The short name found nothing. That isn't an error and it isn't a warning. It's an honest answer to a question nobody meant to ask, because no annotation is called just Inventory. The processor goes on, generates nothing, and the first complaint comes much later, when some code calls a card that was never written.

(The lab's processors write the full name as a string, so you can see it. The smoke example writes Hello::class.qualifiedName!! instead, which lets the compiler catch a typo in the package.)

Ask for an annotation by its full name, and pass the symbol to the logger, so KSP can say where it is.

The helper now knows which boxes to card. Time to write one.

code.title: RungsDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.ksp.l02.demo import com.google.devtools.ksp.ApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.buildApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.KSPLogger import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.Resolver import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessor import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSAnnotated import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSClassDeclaration import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream // The first two rungs of lesson 2's ladder, run together on one MoveMate file in memory: // rung 1: a processor that only says which round it is in // rung 2: a processor that asks for the classes with the sticky note, once by full name and once // (the trap) by short name // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l02.demo.RungsDemoKt /** Rung 1: KSP calls process() once per round; this processor only reports it. */ class RoundLogger(private val logger: KSPLogger) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures: ApiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } private var round = 0 override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { round++ logger.warn("[rung 1] round $round") return emptyList() } } /** Rung 2: find the annotated symbols and log their names. [annotation] is the name it asks for. */ class NoteFinder(private val logger: KSPLogger, private val annotation: String) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures: ApiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { val found = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(annotation).toList() logger.warn("[rung 2] asked for \"$annotation\", found ${found.size}") for (symbol in found) { if (symbol is KSClassDeclaration) logger.warn("[rung 2] found ${symbol.simpleName.asString()}", symbol) } return emptyList() } } private val moveMate = SourceFile.kotlin( "MoveMate.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory @Inventory data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Inventory data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) class Wardrobe(val doors: Int) """, ) fun main() { // all three processors in one compilation: KSP runs them one after the other in every round val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(moveMate) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += SymbolProcessorProvider { env -> RoundLogger(env.logger) } symbolProcessorProviders += SymbolProcessorProvider { env -> NoteFinder(env.logger, "workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") } symbolProcessorProviders += SymbolProcessorProvider { env -> NoteFinder(env.logger, "Inventory") } } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") // the KSP lines only, with the long work-folder path cut down to the file name result.messages.lines().filter { "[ksp]" in it } .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("""/\S*/sources/"""), ".../")) } }

try.expect: The output in this section: [rung 1] round 1, then found 2 with MoveMate.kt:6 for Lamp and MoveMate.kt:9 for Plant, and found 0 for the short name. With the note on the wardrobe, the full name finds 3, and the wardrobe's line is the class Wardrobe line, not the line of its note. The short name still finds 0.

sections.h: Writing the card: createNewFile, Dependencies and a string template
sections.html:
Rung three writes a file. The environment's CodeGenerator creates it, and we write the card's text into it:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: writing a file with javac's Filer
void writeCard(TypeElement cls, String source) throws IOException {
    String pkg = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getPackageOf(cls).getQualifiedName().toString();
    JavaFileObject file = processingEnv.getFiler()
            .createSourceFile(pkg + "." + cls.getSimpleName() + "InventoryCard", cls);  // cls: where it came from
    try (Writer out = file.openWriter()) {
        out.write(source);
    }
}

String cardSource(String pkg, String name, List<String> properties) {
    String pairs = properties.stream()
            .map(p -> "\"" + p + "=\" + thing." + p + "()")          // "name=" + thing.name()
            .collect(Collectors.joining(" + \", \" + "));
    return "package " + pkg + ";\n\n"
            + "public final class " + name + "InventoryCard {\n"
            + "    public static String inventoryCard(" + name + " thing) {\n"
            + "        return \"" + name + ": \" + " + pairs + ";\n"
            + "    }\n"
            + "}\n";
}
Kotlin
fun writeCard(cls: KSClassDeclaration, source: String) {
    val file = cls.containingFile!! // a class from source code always has one
    codeGenerator.createNewFile(
        Dependencies(aggregating = false, file),
        cls.packageName.asString(),
        "${cls.simpleName.asString()}InventoryCard",
    ).use { it.write(source.toByteArray()) }
}

fun cardSource(cls: KSClassDeclaration, properties: List<String>): String {
    val name = cls.simpleName.asString()
    val pairs = properties.joinToString(", ") { "$it=\$$it" } // name=$name: the generated code's own template
    return """
        |// Generated by InventoryProcessor from $name. Do not edit.
        |package ${cls.packageName.asString()}
        |
        |fun $name.inventoryCard(): String =
        |    "$name: $pairs"
        |""".trimMargin()
}

Read writeCard aloud: "make a new file called LampInventoryCard.kt in Lamp's package, note that it comes from Lamp's source file, and write the card's text into it." createNewFile returns an OutputStream, and use closes it when the block ends; KSP picks the file up only once it's closed. The Java version does the same with Filer.createSourceFile, which takes the new class's full name and the elements the file came from.

The properties it receives come from the Read move, one filter in readProperties: the names of the primary constructor's val and var parameters, in order. A plain constructor parameter isn't a property, so a card couldn't read it.

Two lines deserve a second look. The first is the string template inside cardSource. The card we generate contains Kotlin's own $name, so the processor must write a dollar sign without letting its own template expand it. "$it=\$$it" turns name into name=$name: the backslash keeps the second dollar sign for the generated code. That's the first of several small traps in writing code as plain strings, and lesson 4 trades the strings for a library that knows Kotlin's rules.

The second is Dependencies(aggregating = false, file). It tells KSP which source file this output was made from: this card comes from Lamp's file alone. On a later build, KSP uses that to redo only the cards whose files changed. For now, one sentence is enough: name the file each output came from. Lesson 7 shows what goes wrong when you don't.

CardDemo runs the whole lesson 2 processor on two classes in memory, and prints what KSP said and every file it wrote:

exit code: OK
i: [ksp] l02 round 1: @Inventory on [Lamp, Plant]
i: [ksp] l02 round 2: @Inventory on []
--- movemate/LampInventoryCard.kt
// Generated by InventoryProcessor from Lamp. Do not edit.
package movemate

fun Lamp.inventoryCard(): String =
    "Lamp: name=$name, bulbs=$bulbs, shade=$shade"
--- movemate/PlantInventoryCard.kt
// Generated by InventoryProcessor from Plant. Do not edit.
package movemate

fun Plant.inventoryCard(): String =
    "Plant: kind=$kind, potLitres=$potLitres, waterEveryDays=$waterEveryDays"
--- lampCard() returns: Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null

Notice the two i: lines at the top: the processor ran twice. KSP calls process once per round, one pass over the files. A round that writes new files earns another round, in which those files are read too, in case they carry sticky notes of their own. Round 2 asked the same question and got [], because the cards carry no @Inventory. Nothing new was written, so processing ended and the compiler took over. The figure draws those two rounds, and lesson 6 makes rounds the whole topic.

Here the picture bends. A real helper would notice a new card the moment it was written. KSP's helper sees new files only in the next round, and it's the same helper on every pass: KSP creates the processor once per build and calls process again each round.

Rounds set a trap. TwiceDemo has a processor that doesn't ask for annotated symbols. It walks getAllFiles(), every file, in every round, and round 2's files include Lamp.kt again:

exit code: INTERNAL_ERROR
w: [ksp] round 1: getAllFiles() = [Lamp.kt]
w: [ksp] round 2: getAllFiles() = [Lamp.kt, LampInventoryCard.kt]
kotlin.io.FileAlreadyExistsException: .../kotlin/movemate/LampInventoryCard.kt

The helper cheerfully started Lamp's card a second time, and KSP stopped the whole build. A file may be created only once per build, in KSP as in javac, whose Filer throws a FilerException for the same mistake. getSymbolsWithAnnotation protects you here: in each round it returns only symbols from that round's new files, plus any set aside for later.

Write each output once. Ask the resolver for what's new in this round, not for everything.

The happy path works. But a sticky note can land on something that isn't a class at all.

code.html: package workbench.ksp.l02.demo import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l02.InventoryProcessorProvider // Rung 3: the whole @Inventory processor on two MoveMate classes, in memory. Prints what KSP said, every file the // processor wrote, and the result of calling one generated card. Reference processor by default; -Pmine=l02 for yours. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l02.demo.CardDemoKt fun main() { val moveMate = SourceFile.kotlin( "MoveMate.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory @Inventory data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Inventory data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) fun lampCard() = Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null).inventoryCard() """, ) val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(moveMate) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += InventoryProcessorProvider() } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") result.messages.lines().filter { "[ksp]" in it }.forEach(::println) val generated = compilation.kspSourcesDir.resolve("kotlin") generated.walk().filter { it.isFile }.sorted().forEach { file -> println("--- ${file.relativeTo(generated).invariantSeparatorsPath}") print(file.readText()) } if (result.exitCode == KotlinCompilation.ExitCode.OK) { val card = result.classLoader.loadClass("movemate.MoveMateKt").getMethod("lampCard").invoke(null) println("--- lampCard() returns: $card") } }

try.expect: CardDemo prints exit code: OK, the two i: [ksp] l02 round ... lines (round 2 finds []), both card files and lampCard() returns: Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null. TwiceDemo ends with exit code: INTERNAL_ERROR and kotlin.io.FileAlreadyExistsException: .../kotlin/movemate/LampInventoryCard.kt, right after its round 2 line lists Lamp.kt again. An exception thrown inside a processor is an internal error; a logger.error gives a compilation error instead, as the next section shows.

video.title: Your first processor writes the cards: one file per class, a second round that finds nothing new, and why writing a file twice fails

sections.h: When the note is on the wrong thing: an error that points at the exact box
sections.html:
@Inventory can be put on an interface, which has no constructor and no properties to put on a card. The quickest reaction is to throw an exception. That stops the build with a stack trace from inside the processor, which tells the user about our code instead of theirs (lesson 5 shows one). The better reaction is a message on the symbol, which is the Check move:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: javac's Messager, with the element as the location
if (element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS) {
    processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR,
            "@Inventory goes on a class, but " + element.getSimpleName() + " is an " + element.getKind(),
            element);
    continue;
}
Kotlin
fun checkIsClass(symbol: KSAnnotated): KSClassDeclaration? {
    if (symbol is KSClassDeclaration && symbol.classKind == ClassKind.CLASS) return symbol
    logger.error("@Inventory goes on a class, but ${describe(symbol)}", symbol)
    return null
}

classKind tells a class apart from an interface, an object or an enum class. describe is a small given helper that turns the symbol into words, such as "Shape is an interface". The Java twin reads the same fact from getKind().

Put @Inventory interface Shape in the lesson 2 playground and run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin. Here is what it printed, trimmed:

> Task :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin
e: [ksp] /home/user/jvm-workbench/labs/ksp/app/src/l02/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l02/Shape.kt:6: @Inventory goes on a class, but Shape is an interface
e: [ksp] MovingDayJava.java:11: Unresolved reference 'BoxInventoryCardKt'
e: [ksp] MovingDay.kt:24: Unresolved reference 'inventoryCard' on receiver of type 'Box'.
...
> Task :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin FAILED

* What went wrong:
Execution failed for task ':ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin' (registered by plugin 'org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm').
> A failure occurred while executing com.google.devtools.ksp.gradle.KspAAWorkerAction
   > KSP failed with exit code: PROCESSING_ERROR

The first line is the real one. It names the absolute path, the line, and the reason. Line 6 is interface Shape, not line 5, where @Inventory sits: KSP points at the declaration, not at its note.

The lines after it are follow-on errors, about a dozen in the full output. After a failed run, KSP type-checks the code that calls the cards, and the cards were never written. They name only a file, MovingDay.kt:24, without a folder, which is the clue that they aren't the problem to fix first. Then the build fails with KSP failed with exit code: PROCESSING_ERROR.

A logger.error doesn't stop the helper in the middle of the round. The round finishes, so one build can report every bad box at once, and only then does KSP fail the build. In the lab's tests, the same error arrives as text that a test can match: e: [ksp] .../Shape.kt:6: @Inventory goes on a class, but Shape is an interface.

Report a bad box with logger.error on the symbol, never with an exception: the message lands on the user's file and line.

That completes the five moves. Find asks for the full name, Check reports on the symbol, Read takes the constructor's properties, Write creates one file per class, and Prove is the lab.

try.title: Put a note on the wrong box

compare.title: The same first processor, as a javac processor and as a KSP processor

java.title: InventoryProcessor.java
java.html: // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_21) public class InventoryProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { Elements elements = processingEnv.getElementUtils(); TypeElement inventory = elements.getTypeElement("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory"); for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(inventory)) { // 1. Find if (element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS) { // 2. Check processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "@Inventory goes on a class", element); continue; } TypeElement cls = (TypeElement) element; String pkg = elements.getPackageOf(cls).getQualifiedName().toString(); String name = cls.getSimpleName().toString(); try (Writer out = processingEnv.getFiler() // 4. Write .createSourceFile(pkg + "." + name + "InventoryCard", cls).openWriter()) { out.write("package " + pkg + ";\n..."); } catch (IOException e) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, e.toString(), cls); } } return false; } } // registered in META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor

kotlin.title: InventoryProcessor.kt
kotlin.html: class InventoryProcessorProvider : SymbolProcessorProvider { override fun create(environment: SymbolProcessorEnvironment): SymbolProcessor = InventoryProcessor(environment.codeGenerator, environment.logger) } class InventoryProcessor( private val codeGenerator: CodeGenerator, private val logger: KSPLogger, ) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { for (symbol in resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory")) { // 1. Find if (symbol !is KSClassDeclaration || symbol.classKind != ClassKind.CLASS) { // 2. Check logger.error("@Inventory goes on a class", symbol) continue } val names = symbol.primaryConstructor?.parameters.orEmpty() // 3. Read .filter { it.isVal || it.isVar }.map { it.name!!.asString() } codeGenerator.createNewFile( // 4. Write Dependencies(false, symbol.containingFile!!), symbol.packageName.asString(), "${symbol.simpleName.asString()}InventoryCard", ).use { it.write(cardSource(symbol, names).toByteArray()) } } return emptyList() } } // registered in META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider

compare.note: The two processors make the same moves in the same order, and most of the API maps one to one: getElementsAnnotatedWith to getSymbolsWithAnnotation, Messager.printMessage(ERROR, ..., element) to logger.error(..., symbol), Filer.createSourceFile(name, element) to createNewFile(Dependencies(...), package, name). Three differences are real. javac creates its processor through a no-argument constructor, while KSP asks a provider, so a KSP processor can take its tools as constructor parameters. javac returns true or false to "claim" annotations from other processors; KSP has no claiming, and process returns the symbols it set aside for a later round. And the Java version needs a read step of its own to find a constructor, because Java has no primary constructor; lesson 3 shows how much more of the Kotlin label KSP can read.

worked.title: Find out why a processor generates nothing

steps.say: A teammate's build is green, yet LampInventoryCard.kt never appears, and the app fails later with Unresolved reference 'inventoryCard'. First, make the processor say what it sees, at the top of process.
steps.code: override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { val found = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("Inventory").toList() // 1. say what this round found logger.warn("round ${++round}: found ${found.map { (it as KSDeclaration).simpleName.asString() }}") // ... the rest of the processor ... return emptyList() }

alt.html: @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { TypeElement inventory = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getTypeElement("Inventory"); // 1. say what this round found: here getTypeElement returned null processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.WARNING, "round " + (++round) + ": annotation type = " + inventory); return false; }

steps.say: The build prints w: [ksp] round 1: found []. Two facts follow. The processor runs, since a missing services file would have failed with No providers found in processor classpath., and the clipboard came back empty. So the question was wrong, not the house: the short name "Inventory" matches nothing. The Java twin trips earlier and louder, because getTypeElement("Inventory") returns null.
Fix the question with the full name, and the next build prints both rounds: the classes in round 1, and nothing in round 2, once the new cards have been read.
steps.code: // 2. ask by the fully qualified name val found = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory").toList() // w: [ksp] round 1: found [Box, Lamp, Bookshelf, Plant] // w: [ksp] round 2: found []

alt.html: // 2. look the annotation up by its fully qualified name TypeElement inventory = processingEnv.getElementUtils() .getTypeElement("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory"); Set<? extends Element> found = roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(inventory);

steps.say: A warning on every build is noisy for everyone who uses the processor, so lower it to logger.info once it works. Info lines show only when you ask Gradle for them: ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin --rerun --info | grep '\[ksp\]' printed i: [ksp] loaded provider(s): [workbench.ksp.l02.InventoryProcessorProvider] and the lesson 2 processor's own i: [ksp] l02 round 1: @Inventory on [Box, Lamp, Bookshelf, Plant] and round 2: @Inventory on []. --rerun makes Gradle run the task even when nothing changed.

lab.title: The @Inventory card processor, five moves with plain strings
steps: Read InventoryProcessor.kt. The provider, apiFeatures, the process wrapper and the loop in processCards are given. Each function under the loop holds one move and one TODO.

Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin -Pmine=l02. Your processor already runs in a real build: it prints w: [ksp] l02 not done yet: 1. Find: ... and the build passes. Each move you finish moves that message along to the next one. If the task says UP-TO-DATE and prints nothing, add --rerun.
1. Find: in findAnnotated, ask the resolver for workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory, and return the result as a list.
1. Check: in checkIsClass, return the symbol when it's a class (ClassKind.CLASS). Otherwise log @Inventory goes on a class, but ${describe(symbol)} with logger.error, on the symbol, and return null.
1. Read: in readProperties, take the primary constructor's parameters, keep the val and var ones, and return their names in order.

1. Write: build the file's text in cardSource (the comment shows it exactly), then create the file in writeCard with codeGenerator.createNewFile(Dependencies(false, file), package, "${name}InventoryCard").

1. Prove: run the tests until all four pass. Then run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin -Pmine=l02, open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l02/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l02/LampInventoryCard.kt, and run ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l02.MovingDayKt -Pmine=l02.
From memory: close the file, and write the provider class and the services file's one line on paper. Then compare them with the file.
hints: getSymbolsWithAnnotation returns a Sequence; call .toList() so the loop can read it once.
classKind == ClassKind.CLASS is true for a class or a data class, and false for an interface, an object or an enum class.
In cardSource, "$it=\$$it" writes name=$name. A raw string """...""" with trimMargin() keeps the layout readable; inside it, write the generated dollar sign as ${'$'}.
createNewFile returns an OutputStream: .use { it.write(source.toByteArray()) } writes the text and closes the file.
The error must be logged on the symbol, logger.error(message, symbol), or the test can't find Shape.kt:6 in the message.
lab.done: All four tests in InventoryProcessorTest pass, and ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin -Pmine=l02 writes the four card files.

drill.title: Write a first processor from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a provider and a processor that, for each class annotated @Hello (workbench.ksp.annotations.smoke.Hello), writes <Name>Hello.kt in the class's package, holding fun helloFrom<Name>() = "Hello from <Name>". Add the services file's line. Then write the javac version: an AbstractProcessor with getElementsAnnotatedWith and the Filer. Compare with the answer.

answer.html: class HelloProvider : SymbolProcessorProvider { override fun create(environment: SymbolProcessorEnvironment): SymbolProcessor = HelloProcessor(environment.codeGenerator) } class HelloProcessor(private val codeGenerator: CodeGenerator) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { for (cls in resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.smoke.Hello") .filterIsInstance<KSClassDeclaration>()) { val name = cls.simpleName.asString() val pkg = cls.packageName.asString() codeGenerator.createNewFile(Dependencies(false, cls.containingFile!!), pkg, "${name}Hello") .use { it.write("package $pkg\n\nfun helloFrom$name() = \"Hello from $name\"\n".toByteArray()) } } return emptyList() } } // META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider: // workbench.ksp.smoke.HelloProvider

alt.title: HelloProcessor.java
alt.html: @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.smoke.Hello") @SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_21) public class HelloProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { TypeElement hello = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getTypeElement("workbench.ksp.annotations.smoke.Hello"); for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(hello)) { String name = element.getSimpleName().toString(); String pkg = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getPackageOf(element).getQualifiedName().toString(); try (Writer out = processingEnv.getFiler().createSourceFile(pkg + "." + name + "Hello", element).openWriter()) { out.write("package " + pkg + ";\n\npublic final class " + name + "Hello {\n" + " public static String helloFrom" + name + "() { return \"Hello from " + name + "\"; }\n}\n"); } catch (IOException e) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, e.toString(), element); } } return false; } } // META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor: the class's full name

recap: A KSP processor is a provider (SymbolProcessorProvider.create, called once per build), a processor (SymbolProcessor.process) and a services file that names the provider. Without the file: No providers found in processor classpath.
getSymbolsWithAnnotation takes the annotation's fully qualified name. A short name silently finds nothing.
codeGenerator.createNewFile(Dependencies(false, file), package, name) makes one new file. Dependencies names the source file it came from, which incremental builds rely on (lesson 7).
process runs once per round, and a round that writes files earns another round over them. Writing the same file twice fails with FileAlreadyExistsException.
logger.error(message, symbol) reports on the user's file and the declaration's line, lets the round finish, then fails the build with PROCESSING_ERROR.
The limit: plain strings know nothing about Kotlin. A $ must be escaped by hand, and imports, nullable and generic types and awkward names are still ahead (lesson 4).

explain.prompt: Explain, step by step, what happens between typing ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin and the moment LampInventoryCard.kt exists, and why there is a second round.
explain.answer: Gradle first compiles the processor module and packs lesson 2's processor into a jar, with the services file inside it. The KSP task loads that jar, reads the services file, and calls the provider's create once, which builds the processor with the code generator and the logger. Then round 1 starts: KSP calls process with a resolver, the processor asks it for every symbol annotated workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory, checks that each one is a class, reads the names of its constructor's properties, and creates one new file per class with createNewFile, naming the source file it came from. Because round 1 wrote files, KSP runs round 2 over them, in case they carry annotations too. The cards don't, so round 2 finds nothing and writes nothing, and processing ends. Then the Kotlin compiler compiles the app's files and the new cards together.

deeper.html:
Where do a processor's messages show up? KSP's levels follow Gradle's. At the default level you see warn and error lines; info appears with --info, logging only with --debug, and -q hides even warnings. A message logged on a symbol from source gets <absolute path>:<line>: in front of it, with no column. That's why the lab's round lines use logger.info: they're there when you ask, and quiet when you don't.

javac's rounds work almost the same way, with one extra step. javac keeps calling a processor in every later round once it has been asked to process, and it ends with a final round in which roundEnv.processingOver() returns true and no new files will be read. KSP has no such empty round; its end hook is finish(), which lesson 6 uses. javac also lets a processor claim annotations by returning true, so that no other processor sees them. KSP has no claiming at all.

Writing the services file by hand is fine for one provider, but easy to forget when classes are renamed. Many Java libraries use AutoService, which generates META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor from an annotation on the processor class, and a KSP port of it, auto-service-ksp, does the same for KSP providers. A typo in the class name is still possible either way, and the build still names it: Provider ... not found.

One trap from the Java side: since JDK 23, javac no longer runs a processor just because its jar is on the class path. Gradle's annotationProcessor configuration passes processors explicitly, so Gradle builds don't notice, but a plain javac -cp processor.jar command quietly generates nothing until you add --processor-path or -proc:full.
